chapter.name: Thermal Properties of Matter
chapter.blurb: The chapter defines temperature and heat, sets up the Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales and uses the ideal-gas equation to arrive at absolute zero. It then studies what heat does to matter: thermal expansion and thermal stress, specific heat capacity and calorimetry, and changes of state with latent heat. Finally it describes how heat is transferred by conduction, convection and radiation, and how a hot body cools according to Newton's law of cooling.

scope_in.item: Define temperature as a measure of hotness and heat as energy transferred by virtue of temperature difference, with their SI units; explain why two fixed points are needed for a temperature scale
Convert between the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales using (tF - 32)/180 = tC/100, for temperatures and for temperature differences
State Boyle's and Charles' laws and the ideal-gas equation PV = mu R T (R = 8.31 J/mol K); explain the constant-volume gas thermometer, absolute zero (-273.15 degrees C) and use T = tC + 273.15
Use delta l / l = alpha_l delta T for linear expansion and delta A / A = 2 alpha_l delta T for area expansion, including the derivation of the area relation for a rectangular sheet
Explain thermal stress in a rod whose expansion is prevented and calculate the compressive strain, stress and force using Young's modulus
Use delta V / V = alpha_v delta T, derive alpha_v = 3 alpha_l for a cube, and describe how alpha_v varies with temperature for solids, liquids and an ideal gas (alpha_v = 1/T at constant pressure)
Describe the anomalous expansion of water between 0 and 4 degrees C and explain why lakes freeze from the top

Define heat capacity, specific heat capacity and molar specific heat capacity (Cp and Cv for gases) with units, use delta Q = m s delta T, and explain consequences of the high specific heat capacity of water
Apply the principle of calorimetry (heat lost = heat gained in an isolated system) to mixtures and to finding a specific heat capacity with a calorimeter
Describe melting, freezing, vaporisation, boiling and sublimation, the constancy of temperature during a change of state, the effect of pressure on melting and boiling points, and regelation
Describe the pressure-temperature phase diagram (fusion, vaporisation and sublimation curves) and the triple point, with the triple-point temperature of water 273.16 K
Define latent heat, use Q = m L with the latent heats of fusion and vaporisation, interpret the temperature-heat graph for water, and solve problems combining warming and changes of state

Describe conduction and use H = K A (TC - TD)/L for steady-state heat flow, including two bars joined end to end (junction temperature, equivalent conductivity); compare good conductors and insulators
Describe natural and forced convection, including sea and land breezes and trade winds
Describe heat transfer by radiation, the effect of surface colour, and the Dewar flask
Use Wien's displacement law (lambda_m T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K) and the Stefan-Boltzmann law H = A e sigma T^4 and H = e sigma A (T^4 - Ts^4) for blackbody and thermal radiation

State Newton's law of cooling and its limit of validity, use dT2/dt = -K (T2 - T1) and T2 = T1 + C' e^(-Kt), describe its experimental verification, and calculate cooling times by the average-temperature method

concepts.name: Temperature, heat, temperature scales and absolute temperature
concepts.description: Temperature and heat, the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales and their conversion, Boyle's and Charles' laws, the ideal-gas equation, the constant-volume gas thermometer, absolute zero and the Kelvin scale.
concepts.idea: Temperature is a measure of hotness, and heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. A temperature scale needs two fixed points, and low-density gases, which all behave alike, lead to an absolute scale whose zero is at -273.15 degrees C.
concepts.rule: Heat is the form of energy transferred between two (or more) systems, or a system and its surroundings, by virtue of temperature difference; its SI unit is the joule, and the SI unit of temperature is the kelvin. The ice point and steam point of water are 0 degrees C and 100 degrees C on the Celsius scale and 32 degrees F and 212 degrees F on the Fahrenheit scale, so (tF - 32)/180 = tC/100, that is tF = (9/5) tC + 32. For a fixed quantity of low-density gas, PV = constant at constant temperature (Boyle's law) and V/T = constant at constant pressure (Charles' law); together PV = mu R T, where mu is the number of moles and R = 8.31 J/mol K. At constant volume P is proportional to T, which is the basis of the constant-volume gas thermometer. Extrapolating the straight line of P against temperature to zero pressure gives absolute zero, -273.15 degrees C, the zero of the Kelvin scale: T = tC + 273.15, with the same size of unit as the Celsius scale.
concepts.example: A temperature of 40 degrees C is tF = (9/5) x 40 + 32 = 104 degrees F, and T = 40 + 273.15 = 313.15 K.

concepts.name: Linear and area expansion of solids and thermal stress
concepts.description: Thermal expansion of solids in length and in area, the coefficient of linear expansion, the area expansion of a sheet, and the thermal stress set up when expansion is prevented.
concepts.idea: Most substances expand on heating. For a small temperature change the fractional change in length of a rod is proportional to the change in temperature, and if the expansion is prevented by rigid supports a large stress appears in the rod.
concepts.rule: Linear expansion: delta l / l = alpha_l x delta T, where alpha_l is the coefficient of linear expansion (linear expansivity), characteristic of the material, unit K^-1; so l2 = l1 [1 + alpha_l (T2 - T1)]. Metals normally have relatively high values of alpha_l. Area expansion of a sheet: delta A / A = 2 alpha_l x delta T, obtained by neglecting the product alpha_l x delta T in comparison with 2. If a rod is prevented from expanding by fixing its ends rigidly, it acquires a compressive strain delta l / l = alpha_l x delta T; the corresponding thermal stress is delta F / A = Y x alpha_l x delta T, where Y is Young's modulus, and the force is delta F = A Y alpha_l delta T.
concepts.example: A brass rod 2 m long (alpha_l = 1.8 x 10^-5 K^-1) warmed by 30 K lengthens by 2 x 1.8 x 10^-5 x 30 = 1.08 x 10^-3 m, about 1.1 mm.

questions.q: A rectangular sheet of a solid has length a and breadth b. Its temperature rises by delta T and its coefficient of linear expansion is alpha_l. Derive the relation between the coefficient of area expansion, (delta A / A) / delta T, and alpha_l, stating clearly the approximation you make.
questions.a: The length increases by delta a = alpha_l a delta T and the breadth by delta b = alpha_l b delta T. The increase in area is delta A = a delta b + b delta a + (delta a)(delta b) = alpha_l ab delta T + alpha_l ab delta T + (alpha_l)^2 ab (delta T)^2 = alpha_l A delta T (2 + alpha_l delta T), where A = ab. Since alpha_l is of the order of 10^-5 K^-1, the product alpha_l delta T is very small compared with 2 and is neglected. Hence delta A = 2 alpha_l A delta T, that is (delta A / A) / delta T = 2 alpha_l: the coefficient of area expansion is twice the linear expansivity.
s: Writes delta a = alpha_l a delta T, delta b = alpha_l b delta T and delta A = a delta b + b delta a + (delta a)(delta b)
Obtains delta A = alpha_l A delta T (2 + alpha_l delta T) and neglects alpha_l delta T compared with 2
Concludes (delta A / A) / delta T = 2 alpha_l

Acting over the cross-section of a rail this gives a very large force, which can easily bend the rails.
s: Calculates thermal stress = Y alpha_l delta T = 6.0 x 10^7 N/m^2

questions.a: Expansion of one rail = l alpha_l delta T = 12 x 1.2 x 10^-5 x (55 - 15) = 5.76 x 10^-3 m = 5.76 mm, half of it (2.88 mm) at each end. Each gap is closed from both sides, by half the expansion of each of the two neighbouring rails, so the gap needed is 2.88 + 2.88 = 5.76 mm. With no gap the rails could not expand: a compressive thermal stress would be set up and the resulting large force could bend (buckle) the rails.

Gap = half the expansion of each of the two neighbouring rails = 5.76 mm

concepts.name: Volume expansion, the anomalous expansion of water and expansion of gases
concepts.description: The coefficient of volume expansion and its relation to the linear coefficient, the anomalous behaviour of water between 0 and 4 degrees C, and the volume expansion of an ideal gas at constant pressure.
concepts.idea: The fractional change in volume of a substance is proportional to its change in temperature. Water is unusual in contracting when heated from 0 to 4 degrees C, and gases expand far more than solids or liquids.
concepts.rule: Volume expansion: delta V / V = alpha_v x delta T, where alpha_v is the coefficient of volume expansion (K^-1); it is characteristic of the substance but not strictly constant (for copper it becomes constant only at high temperature). For a cube expanding equally in all directions, delta V = (l + delta l)^3 - l^3, which is approximately 3 l^2 delta l, so alpha_v = 3 alpha_l. Water contracts on heating between 0 degrees C and 4 degrees C and has its maximum density at 4 degrees C, so lakes freeze at the top first. For liquids alpha_v is relatively independent of temperature; for an ideal gas at constant pressure P delta V = mu R delta T gives delta V / V = delta T / T, so alpha_v = 1/T, which decreases as temperature increases (about 3.7 x 10^-3 K^-1 at 0 degrees C).
concepts.example: 100 cm^3 of paraffin (alpha_v = 58.8 x 10^-5 K^-1) warmed by 50 K expands by 100 x 58.8 x 10^-5 x 50 = 2.94 cm^3.

concepts.name: Specific heat capacity and calorimetry
concepts.description: Heat capacity, specific heat capacity and molar specific heat capacity (including Cp and Cv of gases), the high specific heat capacity of water and its consequences, and the principle of calorimetry.
concepts.idea: The heat needed to warm a substance depends on its mass, the temperature rise and the nature of the substance. In an isolated system the heat lost by the hotter part equals the heat gained by the colder part.
concepts.rule: Heat capacity S = delta Q / delta T (J/K). Specific heat capacity s = S/m = (1/m)(delta Q / delta T), unit J kg^-1 K^-1, so delta Q = m s delta T when there is no change of state; s depends on the nature of the substance and its temperature. Molar specific heat capacity C = S/mu = (1/mu)(delta Q / delta T), unit J mol^-1 K^-1; for a gas it is Cp if the pressure is held constant and Cv if the volume is held constant. Water has the highest specific heat capacity of the substances tabulated (4186 J/kg K), which is why it is used as a coolant and why it warms more slowly than land. Calorimetry: when no heat escapes to the surroundings, heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the colder body (and its container).
concepts.example: To warm 2 kg of water (s = 4186 J/kg K) by 10 K needs delta Q = m s delta T = 2 x 4186 x 10 = 83720 J.

concepts.name: Change of state: melting, boiling, sublimation, regelation and the triple point
concepts.description: Melting and freezing, vaporisation and boiling, the dependence of melting and boiling points on pressure, regelation, sublimation, and the pressure-temperature phase diagram with its triple point.
concepts.idea: During a change of state the temperature stays constant while the two states coexist in thermal equilibrium, and the temperature at which this happens depends on pressure.
concepts.rule: Solid to liquid is melting (fusion) and liquid to solid is freezing; liquid to vapour is vaporisation. The temperature remains constant until the whole of the substance has changed state: solid and liquid coexist in thermal equilibrium at the melting point, liquid and vapour at the boiling point. Melting and boiling points depend on pressure; their values at standard atmospheric pressure are the normal melting point and normal boiling point. Increased pressure lowers the melting point of ice, and the water refreezes when the pressure is removed (regelation). The boiling point rises when the pressure is increased (pressure cooker) and falls when it is decreased (cooking on hills). Sublimation is the change from solid directly to vapour (dry ice, iodine). On a pressure-temperature phase diagram the fusion, vaporisation and sublimation curves separate the solid, liquid and vapour regions and meet at the triple point, where all three phases coexist; for water its temperature is 273.16 K.
concepts.example: At standard atmospheric pressure ice melts at 0 degrees C and water boils at 100 degrees C; these are the normal melting point and the normal boiling point of water.

concepts.name: Latent heat of fusion and of vaporisation
concepts.description: Latent heat as the heat per unit mass transferred during a change of state, Q = mL, the latent heats of fusion and vaporisation, the temperature-heat graph for water, and calculations that combine warming with changes of state.
concepts.idea: A change of state needs heat even though the temperature does not change. The heat needed is proportional to the mass, and the heat per unit mass is the latent heat of the substance for that change.
concepts.rule: Q = m L, or L = Q/m, where L is the latent heat, a characteristic of the substance; its SI unit is J kg^-1 and its value depends on pressure (usually quoted at standard atmospheric pressure). Lf is the latent heat of fusion (solid-liquid) and Lv the latent heat of vaporisation (liquid-gas). For water Lf = 3.33 x 10^5 J/kg and Lv = 22.6 x 10^5 J/kg. On a graph of temperature against heat supplied, the temperature stays constant during each change of state, and the sloping lines for the different states have different slopes because their specific heat capacities differ. Steam at 100 degrees C carries 22.6 x 10^5 J/kg more heat than water at 100 degrees C. In a calculation, add m s delta T for each stage of warming and m L for each change of state.
concepts.example: To melt 2 kg of lead at its melting point, with Lf = 0.25 x 10^5 J/kg for lead, needs Q = m Lf = 2 x 0.25 x 10^5 = 5.0 x 10^4 J.

concepts.name: Heat transfer by conduction and thermal conductivity
concepts.description: Conduction as heat transfer between adjacent parts of a body, the steady-state heat current through a bar, thermal conductivity, good conductors and insulators, and bars joined end to end.
concepts.idea: In the steady state heat flows along an insulated bar at a constant rate that is greater for a larger area, a larger temperature difference, a shorter length and a better conducting material.
concepts.rule: Conduction is the transfer of heat between two adjacent parts of a body because of their temperature difference. For a bar of length L and uniform cross-section A, with insulated sides and ends maintained at temperatures TC and TD (TC > TD), the steady-state rate of flow of heat (heat current) is H = K A (TC - TD)/L, where K is the thermal conductivity of the material, unit J s^-1 m^-1 K^-1 or W m^-1 K^-1. Metals have large K; wood, glass wool and air have small K; gases are poor conductors. In the steady state the heat current is the same across every cross-section, so for two bars joined end to end K1 A1 (T1 - T0)/L1 = K2 A2 (T0 - T2)/L2. For equal lengths and areas the junction temperature is T0 = (K1 T1 + K2 T2)/(K1 + K2) and the equivalent conductivity of the compound bar is K' = 2 K1 K2/(K1 + K2).
concepts.example: A glass window pane of area 1.0 m^2 and thickness 4 mm (K = 0.8 W/m K) with a temperature difference of 5 K across it conducts H = 0.8 x 1.0 x 5 / 0.004 = 1000 W.

concepts.name: Convection, radiation and blackbody radiation
concepts.description: Natural and forced convection with sea breezes, heat transfer by radiation and the effect of the colour of a surface, the Dewar flask, Wien's displacement law and the Stefan-Boltzmann law with emissivity.
concepts.idea: Convection carries heat by bulk motion of a fluid; radiation carries it by electromagnetic waves and needs no medium. The radiation from a hot body peaks at a shorter wavelength and grows very rapidly in total as the temperature rises.
concepts.rule: Convection is heat transfer by actual motion of matter and is possible only in fluids; it is natural (driven by buoyancy, as in sea and land breezes and the trade winds) or forced (by a pump, as in the human circulatory system). Radiation needs no medium: radiant energy travels as electromagnetic waves at 3 x 10^8 m/s. Black bodies absorb and emit radiant energy better than bodies of lighter colours. Wien's displacement law: lambda_m x T = constant = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K, where lambda_m is the wavelength of maximum energy. Stefan-Boltzmann law: a perfect radiator of area A at absolute temperature T emits energy at the rate H = A sigma T^4, with sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4; for a body of emissivity e, H = A e sigma T^4, and with surroundings at Ts the net rate of loss is H = e sigma A (T^4 - Ts^4).
concepts.example: A blackbody whose emission is maximum at lambda_m = 5.8 x 10^-7 m has T = 2.9 x 10^-3 / 5.8 x 10^-7 = 5000 K.

questions.a: Silvered walls: radiation from the inner wall is reflected back to the contents, and the outer wall similarly reflects back any incoming radiation, so transfer by radiation is reduced. questions.q: A student claims that a room heater warms a room just as well when it is fixed close to the ceiling as when it is placed near the floor. Evaluate this claim using the idea of natural convection.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. In natural convection the heated part of a fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises because of buoyancy, while colder fluid moves in to take its place. With the heater near the floor, the air it warms rises and cooler air replaces it, so a convection cycle carries heat through the whole room. With the heater near the ceiling, the warm air is already at the top and stays there, so no such cycle is set up and the lower part of the room is warmed poorly.

Judgement: wrong - a heater near the ceiling leaves the warm air at the top, so no convection cycle warms the room

concepts.name: Newton's law of cooling
concepts.description: The cooling of a hot body in cooler surroundings, Newton's law of cooling and its limits, the cooling equations, the experimental verification and calculations of cooling time.
concepts.idea: A hot body cools quickly at first and then more and more slowly, because its rate of loss of heat is proportional to how much hotter it is than its surroundings.
concepts.rule: Newton's law of cooling: the rate of loss of heat of a body is directly proportional to the difference of temperature between the body (T2) and its surroundings (T1): -dQ/dt = k (T2 - T1), where k is a positive constant depending on the area and nature of the surface of the body. The law holds good only for small differences of temperature. With dQ = m s dT2, dT2/dt = -K (T2 - T1), where K = k/(m s). Integrating, log_e (T2 - T1) = -K t + c, or T2 = T1 + C' e^(-Kt); a graph of log_e (T2 - T1) against time is a straight line of negative slope. For approximate calculations, (fall in temperature)/(time) = K x (average temperature of the body - temperature of the surroundings).
concepts.example: A body in a room at 25 degrees C cools from 65 degrees C to 55 degrees C in 4 minutes. Its average temperature is 60 degrees C, which is 35 degrees C above the room, so 10/4 = K x 35 and K = 1/14 per minute.

questions.a: Integrating dT2/(T2 - T1) = -K dt gives log_e (T2 - T1) = -K t + c, where c is a constant. This has the form y = m x + c with y = log_e (T2 - T1) and x = t, so the graph is a straight line. Its slope is -K, that is the slope is negative and its magnitude is K = k/(m s).
s: Integrates to log_e (T2 - T1) = -K t + c

questions.q: Hot water in a room at 20 degrees C cools from 84 degrees C to 52 degrees C in 6 minutes. Assuming T2 = T1 + C' e^(-Kt), find the further time it takes to cool from 52 degrees C to 28 degrees C, and explain why assuming a constant rate of cooling would give a wrong answer.
questions.a: Work with the excess temperature T2 - T1 = C' e^(-Kt). The excess is 84 - 20 = 64 degrees C at the start and 52 - 20 = 32 degrees C after 6 minutes, so it halves every 6 minutes. At 28 degrees C the excess is 8 degrees C: 32 to 16 takes 6 minutes and 16 to 8 takes another 6 minutes, so the further time is 12 minutes. A constant rate of 32 degrees C per 6 minutes would predict only 24/(32/6) = 4.5 minutes; this is wrong because the rate of cooling decreases as the excess temperature falls.

Excess halves every 6 minutes, so 32 to 8 takes 12 minutes
Explains that the rate of cooling falls as the excess falls, so a constant-rate estimate (4.5 minutes) is too small

Here the difference is 770 degrees C, which is very large, so the rate of loss of heat is not simply proportional to the temperature difference and the prediction would be unreliable.

questions.a: Procedure: note the room temperature, then record the temperature of the stirred water at two times a few minutes apart, and use (fall in temperature)/(time) = K x (average temperature - room temperature). With the readings: average = 66 degrees C, excess = 36 degrees C, rate = 8/4 = 2 degrees C per minute, so K = 2/36 = 1/18 per minute. Prediction: from 50 to 46 degrees C the average is 48 degrees C, excess 18 degrees C, rate = 18/18 = 1 degree C per minute, so the time for a 4 degree fall is 4 minutes. Precaution/assumption: stir gently so the thermometer shows the temperature of all the water; keep the surroundings at a steady temperature; use short temperature intervals and a small excess so that the average-temperature form of the law is valid.

Predicted time = 4/(18/18) = 4 minutes
A sensible precaution or assumption (stirring, steady surroundings, small temperature intervals)
